Film still. Wide shot, locked-off, low eye level, looking along a shallow stream that runs through the glass gallery of a winter garden. Empty of people. Film still. The entire frame is a single undifferentiated white substance. There is no object, no floor, no wall, no ceiling, no horizon, no edge, no corner, no seam, no near and no far. Two faint vertical processing streaks run down the frame. The image is very slightly underexposed for a white, so the white sits just below paper-white and holds density rather than clipping.

The room is a hotel dining room that has become a machine hall along its left side without any break: on the right, moulded panelling, a serving sideboard and round tables with cloths; on the left, riveted steel plate replaces the panelling mid-wall, a cast-iron flywheel two metres across stands where a table would be, and a pipe runs out of the cornice and down into the floor. The transition line crosses the room diagonally and does not follow a wall, a beam or a floor seam.

The composition is unbalanced on purpose: the heavy flywheel sits low in the left third and fills the bottom corner; the right two thirds are almost empty floor with one small chair far off; the ceiling takes the top third and holds nothing. A serving trolley is cut in half by the right frame edge, only its front wheels and one shelf visible. A hanging lamp cord enters the top of the frame and its lamp is above the frame line, out of shot. No object is centred, nothing is mirrored, and the two halves of the frame do not answer each other.

The room is furnished and used: five round tables at unequal spacing, none aligned, cloths hanging crookedly; nine bentwood chairs, two of them tipped forward against the tables; a stack of plates on the sideboard; a dented enamel jug; two oil cans and a rag on the machine side; a wall board whose printed lines are pseudo-alphabetic and never resolve into words, though its numerals are legible and read 10:10.

The quiet failures: the panelling's moulding profile changes twice along its length and back again; three bentwood chairs are the same chair copied, down to the same crack in the same joint; the jug's shadow falls toward the sconce; the floorboards restart their run twice and the seams refuse to meet; the pipe entering the floor has no hole around it.

Underexposed by one and a half stops, deep black in the centre of the room and the ceiling, slow exposure drift across the take, hard local clipping where the raking light strikes the flywheel rim. Dye-density color: dominant cold iron grey, one cutting accent of dirty cream in the tablecloths, matte, no sheen on the metal, heavy muted midtones.

Film still. Extreme wide, locked-off, eye level, shot from the stage out into the auditorium of a small opera house at night, empty of people. No daylight: two high side windows are black, showing nothing — unpainted darkness with a faint canvas weave where an outside was never generated.

The furthest rows are a proper theatre: red plush seats in curved rows, gilded box fronts, a painted ceiling rosette. Ten metres closer to the camera the room has become an operating theatre without any break — the plush seats turn to tiered wooden observation benches mid-row, one seat half plush and half scrubbed pine, the gilt boxes flatten into white tiled walls, and a cast-iron surgical rail runs where the balcony front was. The space is crowded and used: an anatomical skeleton on a stand at the end of a bench row, two enamel instrument trolleys, a rolled screen, satchels hanging on desk hooks, chalk and a folded cloth on the nearest desk, a wall chart of a human figure whose annotation lettering is pseudo-alphabetic and never resolves into words, though its numbered callouts are legible.

Light comes only from practical sources: a single surgical dome lamp above the middle tier, cold and hard, throwing one bright circle onto the benches; the theatre's safety light low on the far wall, weak and amber; and two green desk lamps on the classroom desks in the foreground. Film still. Extreme wide, locked-off, eye level, dead center down the nave of a cathedral at night, empty of people. No daylight anywhere in the frame: every window is black, showing no city, no sky, no stars — unpainted darkness with a faint canvas weave where an outside was never generated, the tall stained glass reading only as dim lead tracery lit from inside the room.

Twenty metres in, without a wall or a door, the cathedral becomes a nineteenth-century railway station concourse: the clustered gothic shafts thin into riveted iron uprights mid-height, the ribbed vault opens into a glazed barrel canopy that shows the same black nothing above it, the flagstone floor turns to soot-blackened platform paving mid-slab with the stone joint continuing across both materials. Along the right aisle the building becomes a third thing: a library reading room, eight long oak tables in rows with green glass banker's lamps, book stacks rising into the triforium arches, rolling ladders on rails that end mid-wall.

The room is crowded and used: forty dark pews, a brass lectern, three iron candle stands with half-burnt candles, a confessional, stacked chairs against a pier, two wooden station benches, a porter's trolley with strapped suitcases, a mop bucket, book carts loaded with volumes, reading chairs pushed back from the tables.

Light comes only from practical sources inside the room: nine lit candles on the stands and the lectern in the foreground; the green banker's lamps down the right aisle, warm and low, pooling on the tables and leaving the stacks above them dark; cold uplight from the station half washing backwards along the iron uprights; and an illuminated hanging departure board whose rows are pseudo-alphabetic characters that never resolve into words, though every time beside them is legible and reads 10:10.
